title: Syncopation, Tuplets and Polyrhythm
intro: Rhythm becomes interesting when it pulls against the meter. Syncopation stresses weak beats, tuplets fit the 'wrong' number of notes into a beat, and polyrhythm runs two different pulses at once.

blocks.text: A syncopation is an accent where the meter does not expect one: on a weak beat, on an offbeat (the 'and'), or a long note that starts on a weak part of the beat and holds through a strong one. The pattern short–long–short (eighth, quarter, eighth) in 4/4 is the classic example: the quarter starts on the 'and' of a beat and covers the next beat.

A tuplet squeezes a different number of equal notes into a span. The triplet, three in the time of two, is by far the most common: three triplet eighths fill one quarter-note beat. Quintuplets (5 in the time of 4) and sextuplets appear in Romantic piano music; a duplet (2 in the time of 3) does the reverse in compound meter.

In swing (jazz, blues, shuffle), pairs of written eighth notes are played long–short, roughly like the first and third notes of a triplet. The exact ratio varies with tempo and player, from nearly even at fast tempos to about 2:1 at medium ones.

A hemiola regroups six beats from two groups of three into three groups of two, so two bars of 3/4 briefly sound like one bar of 3/2. Baroque and Classical composers used it to slow the pulse just before a cadence; it is everywhere in Brahms.

A polyrhythm sounds two pulses at once that divide the same span differently: 3 against 2, 4 against 3. The plot shows where each stream's notes fall in one cycle. Notes coincide only at the start of the cycle (when the two numbers share no common factor); in between they interleave in a fixed pattern.

widget.title: Polyrhythm: a against b over one cycle

blocks.text: To play 3 against 2 at the piano, think of the cycle as six fast pulses: the hand playing 3 strikes on pulses 1, 3 and 5; the hand playing 2 on pulses 1 and 4. The combined rhythm is 'ONE – two-and three' (the phrase 'NICE cup of tea' fits 3 against 2). For 4 against 3, count twelve pulses: the 4-stream lands on 1, 4, 7 and 10 and the 3-stream on 1, 5 and 9.
(The example plays the combined rhythm: the low C is the 2-stream, the rising high notes the 3-stream.)

blocks.title: Triplets
blocks.text: In 4/4 at 120 BPM, how long is one triplet eighth note?
solution: A beat is 60/120 = 0.5 s. Three triplet eighths share one beat, so each lasts 0.5/3 ≈ 0.167 s.

blocks.title: Polyrhythm grid
blocks.text: For 5 against 4, how many grid pulses make one cycle, and on which pulses do the 4-stream notes fall?
solution: The least common multiple of 5 and 4 is 20 pulses. The 4-stream strikes every 5 pulses: on pulses 1, 6, 11 and 16 (counting from 1). The 5-stream strikes every 4: 1, 5, 9, 13 and 17.
